content: Epilepsy is a prevalent neurological disorder, with an estimated incidence of 50 cases per 100,000 individuals. Patients with epilepsy may exhibit various immunological abnormalities, including reduced levels of serum immunoglobulin A (IgA), deficiencies in specific subclasses of immunoglobulin G (IgG), and the presence of certain antibodies. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) therapy has been proposed as a potentially beneficial treatment option, with significant implications for the management of epilepsy. This document represents an updated review of the Cochrane analysis, initially published in 2011 and last revised in 2017. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of IVIg on seizure frequency and duration, quality of life, and adverse effects when used either as a standalone treatment (monotherapy) or as an adjunctive therapy (add-on) for individuals with epilepsy. For the most recent update, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases and registries, including the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS Web), MEDLINE, Web of Science, ISRCTN registry, WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), and ClinicalTrials.gov, with the search completed on December 20, 2018. Reference lists of relevant articles were also reviewed. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials investigating the use of IVIg as monotherapy or add-on therapy in epilepsy patients. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of trials and extracted data. Study authors were contacted for additional information when necessary. The outcomes of interest included the percentage of participants achieving seizure freedom, a reduction in seizure frequency by 50% or more, adverse effects, treatment discontinuation, and quality of life measures. The review included a single study involving 61 participants. This study was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial that compared the efficacy of IVIg as an add-on therapy to a placebo add-on in patients with drug-resistant epilepsy. The study did not report on seizure freedom as an outcome. There was no statistically significant difference between the IVIg group and the placebo group in achieving a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency (risk ratio [RR] 1.89, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.85 to 4.21; one study, 58 participants; low-certainty evidence). However, the study did report a statistically significant improvement in global assessment favoring IVIg (RR 3.29, 95% CI 1.13 to 9.57; one study, 60 participants; low-certainty evidence). No adverse effects were observed in the study. The review did not identify any randomized controlled trials evaluating the use of IVIg as monotherapy for epilepsy. The included study was assessed as having a low to unclear risk of bias. Using the GRADE methodology, the certainty of the evidence was rated as low. In conclusion, the current evidence does not allow for reliable conclusions regarding the efficacy of IVIg as a treatment for epilepsy. Further high-quality randomized controlled trials are necessary to better understand the potential role of IVIg in epilepsy management.
